data.title: Columbia Total Return Municipal Income Fund Q2 2026 Commentary
data.description:
Fund performance

  • Institutional Class shares of Columbia Total Return Municipal Income Fund returned 3.33% for the three months ending June 30, 2026.
  • The fund's benchmark, the Bloomberg Municipal Bond Index, returned 2.50% for the same period.
  • The fund outperformed its benchmark, with a longer-than-benchmark duration profile and exposure to not-rated bonds the primary drivers of the outperformance. (Duration is a measure of a bond's sensitivity to changes in interest rates.)

Market overview

Market volatility continued during the second quarter, as investors navigated persistent inflation pressures, shifting expectations for U.S. Federal Reserve policy and ongoing geopolitical developments in the Middle East. Economic data remained generally resilient, while still-high energy prices and elevated inflation readings led investors to reassess the likelihood of additional rate cuts. Against this backdrop, the Fed left the federal funds rate unchanged at 3.50%–3.75% during its June meeting, with recently confirmed Chairman Kevin Warsh signaling a more cautious and somewhat more hawkish policy stance.

Second-quarter returns were positive across most asset classes. U.S. equities rebounded strongly, led by growth and small-cap stocks, as risk sentiment improved and artificial intelligence (AI)-related spending continued to support technology shares. The broad U.S. investment-grade taxable bond market (Bloomberg Aggregate Bond Index) gained 0.67%, while the Bloomberg US Treasury Index and Bloomberg US Corporate Bond Index returned 0.32% and 1.40%, respectively. The Bloomberg Municipal Bond Index outperformed most major fixed-income indices, returning 2.50% for the quarter, supported by declining municipal yields, strong reinvestment demand and continued inflows into mutual funds, exchange traded funds (ETFs) and separately managed accounts (SMAs).

The municipal market recovered sharply from March's 2.32% rate-driven selloff. April began the quarter with a strong 1.15% rebound, as investors took advantage of higher yields and more compelling relative value. May extended the market's recovery, as risk sentiment improved, and interest rate volatility moderated. June bookended the quarter with a 0.96% return, as favorable summer technicals, reinvestment cash and robust investor demand outweighed another heavy month of new issuance. The result was a broad-based rally that left municipals higher for all three months of the quarter and pushed year-to-date returns to a solidly positive 2.32%.

Municipal yields declined across the yield curve during the quarter, even as Treasury yields moved higher. The municipal rally was led by longer maturities, as yields on bonds 15 years and longer fell by at least 25 basis points (bps). (A basis point is 1/100 of a percent.) The municipal yield curve remained positively sloped, although it flattened modestly, as long-term yields outperformed. Municipal/Treasury yield ratios richened across the curve, with the 2-, 5- and 10-year ratios ending the quarter at 57%, 62% and 66%, respectively, while the 30-year ratio closed the period at 85%. The 10-year Treasury yield ended the month at 4.44%, while the 10-year municipal yield was 2.95%.

Municipal market performance was positive across maturity, quality and sector. The Bloomberg Municipal Bond Index returned 2.50% for the quarter, with longer-maturity and lower-rated bonds outperforming their shorter-maturity and higher-quality counterparts. The Bloomberg Municipal 3-Year, 10-Year and Long Bond (22+ Year) Indices returned 0.83%, 1.90% and 4.24%, respectively, while the Bloomberg Municipal AAA, A and High Yield Indices gained 2.49%, 2.55% and 3.35%, respectively. Performance was supported by declining long-term yields, stable credit spreads, strong carry and demand that continued to absorb elevated supply.

Quarterly portfolio recap

The fund outperformed its benchmark and Morningstar peer group during the second quarter. The fund's outperformance was largely driven by duration/curve positioning and sector allocation, with a partial offset from modest underperformance in security selection.

Duration and curve contributions to benchmark-relative returns were additive, as despite a volatile quarter, municipal yields ended the period lower. Yields were broadly lower across the municipal curve, with yields on 5-, 10- and 30-year bonds lower by 8, 17 and 28 bps, respectively. The longer-intermediate portion of the curve, points between 17 and 22 years to maturity, saw the significant declines in yield, between 30–35 bps. The fund's longer duration profile, with an overweight to the long end of the curve, was additive for the period.

Quality allocation, with a bias toward lower investment grade and an allocation to high yield and not-rated bonds, was positive relative to the benchmark. The high yield segment outperformed investment grade for the quarter, and the fund's modest allocation to high yield and overweight to BBB-rated credits aided relative performance. Sector allocation saw positive contributions from overweights to continuing care retirement community (CCRC), charter schools and prepay gas, while the fund's housing overweight detracted. Security selection was slightly negative, as weaker issue selection within tobacco, local general obligation (GO) and CCRCs more than offset positive security selection within toll roads, special tax, housing and prepay gas.

Portfolio activity

Portfolio activity skewed slightly toward more purchases than sales for the quarter, as the team modestly reduced liquidity in favor of still-attractive yields in the longer-intermediate portion of the curve. Additions were made across several sectors, including housing, prepay gas, charter schools, airports and CCRCs. Sales generally followed the theme of reducing positions with limited further upside potential in favor of better total return opportunities, which included sales within airports, CCRCs, charter schools and local GOs. Sector positioning remained little changed quarter-over-quarter, as more issuer-specific relative value trades were identified than broad sector-based opportunities.

Outlook

The second quarter reinforced the municipal market's strong technical foundation and its ability to produce attractive total returns despite rate volatility and heavy issuance. Demand from retail investors, mutual funds, ETFs and SMAs remained robust, while municipal fundamentals continued to be supported by healthy reserves, resilient tax collections and stable issuer balance sheets. Looking ahead, the remainder of 2026 is expected to remain active and opportunity-rich, although performance will depend on rate volatility, yield-curve positioning, supply absorption and credit differentiation:

  • Rates/yield curve: With the Fed on hold and investors now considering a more hawkish policy path, short-term Treasury yields may remain anchored by policy expectations, while long-term rates remain sensitive to inflation, energy prices and deficits. A still-steep municipal yield curve continues to reward selective extension, particularly where longer maturities offer attractive carry and roll-down potential.
  • Supply/demand: Issuance is on pace for another record year, with first-half volume near $295 billion and second-quarter volume the largest on record. Although supply is likely to stay elevated, reinvestment demand, mutual fund and ETF inflows, and strong SMA demand should help the market absorb issuance without sustained valuation pressure.
  • Credit: Municipal credit fundamentals remain healthy, supported by reserves, stable tax collections and generally conservative budgeting. However, dispersion is increasing, and some sectors — including healthcare, private higher education, mass transit and certain project-finance credits — may remain under pressure.
  • Geopolitics and energy: Middle East developments, energy-market volatility and fiscal-policy uncertainty remain potential sources of inflation and rate volatility. Municipals' defensive characteristics and tax-exempt income may remain attractive during periods of broader market uncertainty.
  • Politics and policy: Municipal/Treasury yield ratios richened in the quarter, making security selection and structure increasingly important. Policy debates around federal funding, tax policy and the municipal tax exemption warrant continued monitoring, as legislation and the news cycle shape market outcomes. In addition, one should be prepared for increased volatility as we move closer to the November mid-term elections.

While additional price appreciation is possible, total returns are likely to be driven primarily by income, carry and yield-curve positioning rather than broad-based spread compression. The fund remains selective, emphasizing credits and structures where compensation appropriately reflects both interest-rate and credit risks.

The fund invests substantially in municipal securities and will be affected by tax, legislative, regulatory, demographic or political changes, as well as changes impacting a state's financial, economic or other conditions. A relatively small number of tax-exempt issuers may necessitate the fund investing more heavily in a single issuer and, therefore, be more exposed to the risk of loss than a fund that invests more broadly. Prepayment and extension risk exists because the timing of payments on a loan, bond or other investment may accelerate when interest rates fall or decelerate when interest rates rise which may reduce investment opportunities and potential returns. Non-investment-grade (high-yield or junk) securities present greater price volatility and more risk to principal and income than higher rated securities. Market risk may affect a single issuer, sector of the economy, industry or the market as a whole. A rise in interest rates may result in a price decline of fixed-income instruments held by the fund, negatively impacting its performance and NAV. Falling rates may result in the fund investing in lower yielding debt instruments, lowering the fund's income and yield. These risks may be heightened for longer maturity and duration securities.
